Daniel’s “self-weight of the water in the maze” explanation implicitly treats the filled path as if it were a single static column whose own hydrostatic head can counter the tank, but in an *open, continuously connected* liquid network hydrostatic pressure is not an extra resisting force—it is the bookkeeping that guarantees consistency. If the water in the maze remained hydraulically connected to the outlet with a continuous liquid phase and vented air, the system would behave like communicating vessels: the reservoir would keep draining until the free surfaces equilibrated at the outlet level, regardless of how tortuous the route is. The mere fact that one segment sits lower than another doesn’t create a net “push back” beyond the ordinary head difference that is already driving flow.

What Daniel’s framing omits—yet is precisely what Steve gestures at with “aggregate surface tension”—is the existence of *interfaces* (menisci) and trapped air that break the simple communicating-vessels picture. Once parts of the maze become separated by air pockets or by pinning at corners/roughness, flow requires pushing a meniscus through constrictions, and that introduces a threshold pressure via the [Young–Laplace equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young%E2%80%93Laplace_equation) (capillary pressure). In small channels, that threshold can easily correspond to centimeters to tens of centimeters of water head, so the reservoir can retain water even while a lower exit exists. A clean way to discriminate the mechanisms is experimental: widen the channels or add a surfactant (lowering surface tension) and the “stuck” head should shrink markedly; if Daniel’s self-weight story were sufficient on its own, those changes would not matter much. For a readable treatment of this classical capillarity lineage (Laplace, Gibbs, modern wetting physics), see de Gennes et al., *Capillarity and Wetting Phenomena* ([Springer](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-21656-0)).
